summary.text: For a prime \(p\), counting pairs divisible by \(p^i\) gives the numerator valuation \(\sum_i \lfloor N/p^i\rfloor^2\), while Legendre’s formula and rearrangement give the denominator valuation \(\sum_i\sum_{r\le m_i} r\lfloor m_i/r\rfloor\), where \(m_i=\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor\); the bound \(r\lfloor m_i/r\rfloor\le m_i\) also proves exact divisibility, so the quotient valuation depends only on the \(m_i\). Since \(\lfloor(np+k)/p^i\rfloor=\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor\) for every \(i\ge1\) when \(0\le k<p\), the required valuations are equal.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 U_N=\prod_{j=1}^{N}\prod_{r=1}^{N}\gcd(j,r),
 \qquad
 D_N=\prod_{r=1}^{N}\left(\left\lfloor\frac Nr\right\rfloor!\right)^r.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
 a(N)=\frac{U_N}{D_N}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and then obtain a formula for its prime-adic valuation.

For a prime \(q\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in a positive integer \(x\). We begin with the numerator.

### 1. The valuation of the numerator

For positive integers \(j,r\),
\[
 v_q(\gcd(j,r))
 =\#\{i\ge 1:q^i\mid j\text{ and }q^i\mid r\}.
\]
Indeed, if \(v_q(j)=s\) and \(v_q(r)=t\), then the right side is the number of positive integers \(i\le \min(s,t)\), namely \(\min(s,t)=v_q(\gcd(j,r))\).

Taking valuations in the product defining \(U_N\), and then interchanging the finite sums, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_q(U_N)
 &=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sum_{r=1}^{N}v_q(\gcd(j,r))\\
 &=\sum_{i\ge1}\#\{(j,r):1\le j,r\le N,\ q^i\mid j,\ q^i\mid r\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are exactly \(\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor\) multiples of \(q^i\) between \(1\) and \(N\), so the number of ordered pairs is its square. Hence
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
 v_q(U_N)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.}
\tag{1}
\]
This is a finite sum because the summands vanish once \(q^i>N\). In particular, it can be written with \(1\le i\le N\), since \(q\ge2\) implies \(q^i>N\) for every \(i>N\).

### 2. The valuation of the denominator

Legendre's formula states that for every nonnegative integer \(M\),
\[
 v_q(M!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{M}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Applying this to each factor of \(D_N\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_q(D_N)
 &=\sum_{r=1}^{N}r\,v_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac Nr\right\rfloor!\right)\\
 &=\sum_{r=1}^{N}r\sum_{i\ge1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/r\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor\\
 &=\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{r=1}^{N}r
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/r\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
For positive integers \(r,d\), successive integer division satisfies
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/r\rfloor}{d}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{N}{rd}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/d\rfloor}{r}\right\rfloor.
\tag{3}
\]
For completeness, this follows directly from the characterization of a floor: an integer \(t\) is at most either side exactly when \(trd\le N\).

For each \(i\ge1\), put
\[
 m_i(N,q)=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Using (3), the inner summand in (2) becomes
\[
 r\left\lfloor\frac{m_i(N,q)}r\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(r>m_i(N,q)\), this is zero. Therefore the upper limit \(N\) may be replaced by \(m_i(N,q)\), and
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
 v_q(D_N)=\sum_{i\ge1}T(m_i(N,q)),
 \qquad
 T(m):=\sum_{r=1}^{m}r\left\lfloor\frac mr\right\rfloor.}
\tag{4}
\]
As in (1), all terms with \(i>N\) vanish.

A key consequence is that \(D_N\) divides \(U_N\). For every \(m\ge0\) and every \(1\le r\le m\),
\[
 r\left\lfloor\frac mr\right\rfloor\le m.
\]
There are \(m\) terms in the definition of \(T(m)\), and hence
\[
 T(m)\le m^2.
\tag{5}
\]
Comparing (4), (5), and (1), prime by prime, gives
\[
 v_q(D_N)
 =\sum_{i\ge1}T(m_i(N,q))
 \le\sum_{i\ge1}m_i(N,q)^2
 =v_q(U_N)

after applying (5) separately for every \(i\). Both \(U_N\) and \(D_N\) are positive: all gcd factors in \(U_N\) have positive arguments, and all factorial factors in \(D_N\) are positive. By unique prime factorization, the inequalities
\(v_q(D_N)\le v_q(U_N)\) for all primes \(q\) imply
\[
 D_N\mid U_N.
\]
Thus \(a(N)=U_N/D_N\) is indeed an integer, and
\[
 v_q(a(N))=v_q(U_N)-v_q(D_N).
\tag{6}
\]
Combining (1), (4), and (6), we could write explicitly
\[
 v_q(a(N))
 =\sum_{i\ge1}
 \left(
 m_i(N,q)^2-T(m_i(N,q))
 \right).
\tag{7}
\]
The important point is that, for a fixed prime \(q\), the valuation \(v_q(a(N))\) depends on \(N\) only through the collection of quotients
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad i\ge1.
\]

To make this dependence completely explicit without using infinite notation, suppose \(N,M\le B\) and
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{M}{q^i}\right\rfloor
 \quad(1\le i\le B).
\tag{8}
\]
The formulas (1) and (4) may both be summed from \(i=1\) to \(B\): any newly appended terms are zero, since if \(i>N\), then \(q^i>N\), and likewise for \(M\). Equation (8) consequently gives both
\[
 v_q(U_N)=v_q(U_M)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 v_q(D_N)=v_q(D_M).
\]
Subtracting as in (6), we conclude that
\[
 v_q(a(N))=v_q(a(M)).
\tag{9}
\]

### 3. Constancy on the block from \(np\) to \(np+p-1\)

Now let \(n\) be a positive integer, let \(p\) be prime, and let \(k\) satisfy \(0\le k<p\). Set
\[
 N_0=np,
 \qquad
 N_1=np+k.
\]
We claim that for every \(i\ge1\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{N_0}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{N_1}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{10}
\]
For \(i=1\), Euclidean division gives
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor=n
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor,
\]
because \(0\le k<p\).

For a general \(i\ge1\), write \(p^i=p\,p^{i-1}\) and use successive integer division. We get
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 &=\left\lfloor
 \frac{\left\lfloor(np+k)/p\right\rfloor}{p^{i-1}}
 \right\rfloor\\
 &=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor,
\end{aligned}
\]
while similarly
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor
 \frac{\left\lfloor np/p\right\rfloor}{p^{i-1}}
 \right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor.
\]
This proves (10).

Finally take \(q=p\), \(N=N_0\), \(M=N_1\), and, for example, \(B=N_1\). We have \(N_0\le N_1=B\), and (10) supplies all the floor equalities required in (8). Therefore (9) yields
\[
 v_p(a(np))=v_p(a(np+k)).
\]
This holds for every \(k\) with \(0\le k<p\). Consequently
\[
 v_p(a(np))=v_p(a(np+1))=\cdots=v_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
which is exactly the stated conjecture.
